What you are experiencing isn't a lack of ability; it’s a standard data-processing bottleneck. Standard sheet music is a highly dense, spatial user interface. If the lines are blurring together, your brain is working overtime just to decode the telemetry of the staff before you can even think about the timing or execution.

Your workaround—extracting the raw data, translating it into a linear sequence of letters, and using your ears for the temporal playback—is a classic engineering approach to a messy interface. It actually maps perfectly to the "Music as sequence of letters" chunking strategy you drew on your whiteboard.

If you want to bridge the gap and learn to read the music directly without the exhausting pencil-counting, we need to change how you look at the page.

1. Stop Decoding Notes; Start Decoding Intervals (Distance)

Right now, you are treating every single note like an isolated variable you have to solve for. Experienced sight-readers don't actually read the letters $A, B, C$; they read spatial relationships (intervals).

The staff is just a grid of lines and spaces:

  • Line to the very next Space (or vice versa) = A step of 2nd (e.g., $C$ to $D$). Your hand just moves to the very next white key.
  • Line to the very next Line (or Space to Space) = A skip of a 3rd (e.g., $C$ to $E$). Your hand skips a key.
  • Line to Line with one line omitted = A jump of a 5th (e.g., $C$ to $G$).

The Hack: When you look at a chord, don't read the three individual notes. Look at the shape of the stack. A standard root triad (like a $C$ major chord) looks like three snowmen blocks perfectly stacked line-line-line or space-space-space. The moment your eyes recognize that visual pattern, your hand automatically maps to a "skip-a-finger" shape on the keys.

2. Establish "Tracer" Anchor Notes

Instead of memorizing all 30+ possibilities on the grand staff, just burn three anchor points into your brain. Think of these as your orientation telemetry. If you know exactly where these are instantly, you can find any other note by just measuring the distance (intervals) from them.

  • Middle C: Floating on its own little ledger line right between the two staves.
  • Treble G (The G Clef): The curly target of the Treble Clef explicitly loops around the second line from the bottom. That line is always $G$.
  • Bass F (The F Clef): The two dots of the Bass Clef sandwich the second line from the top. That line is always $F$.

If you see a note sitting just above the $G$ line, don't count from the bottom up. Your brain goes: "That's one space above my $G$ anchor. It's an $A$."

3. Staging the Practice: Decouple Pitch from Rhythm

Trying to figure out what the chord is at the exact same time you are trying to figure out when to play it is causing your system to crash. You are trying to run two heavy processing threads simultaneously.

Drop the tempo to zero and decouple them entirely:

  • Pass 1 (Pitch Only): Don't use a metronome. Don't worry about rhythm. Just look at the sheet music and place your hands on the chord shapes. Let your eyes adjust to how a visual "skip" on the paper feels like a physical "skip" under your fingers.
  • Pass 2 (Rhythm Only): Close the piano lid or tap on your lap. Look at the notes and just tap out the rhythm. Master the timing curve without the friction of finding the keys.
  • Pass 3 (The Merge): Bring them together at an incredibly slow, deliberate speed.

Since your current sequence-writing method is what actually gets results right now, we can use it as a bridge. Next time you translate a song into a sequence of letters, try keeping the sheet music right next to it.

As you play the letter sequence, force your eyes to look back at the "snowman" shape on the staff. Over time, your brain will start associating the physical shape of the chord under your hands with the visual cluster on the lines, and the blurring will stop.

Here is a structural framework for how that V1 data payload can be modeled to keep it lightweight, easily parseable, and directly useful for your piano workflow.

Designing the V1 Data Payload

To preserve both the pitch data and the linear timeline, the array needs to map characters to standard scientific pitch notation (where Middle C is $C_4$).

Because piano music handles simultaneous events (chords), your array elements should be able to hold either a single note string or an inner array of strings representing a chord played at that specific time step.

System Architecture

[ Raw Sheet Music Image ] 
           │
           ▼
[ OMR / Detection Engine ] (Extracts pitches & time-slices)
           │
           ▼
[ Normalized V1 Data Payload ] (The arrays below)
           │
           ▼
[ Custom Visual Layout Engine ] (Your future human-readable UI)

The V1 JSON Schema Structure

Separating by hand is crucial because your brain processes the left hand (bass clef) and right hand (treble clef) as two distinct motor channels.

{
  "song_metadata": {
    "title": "Timing Project V1",
    "time_signature": "4/4"
  },
  "right_hand_tracks": [
    ["E5"], ["G5"], [["C5", "E5", "G5"]], ["Rest"]
  ],
  "left_hand_tracks": [
    ["C3"], ["G3"], [["C3", "E3", "G3"]], [["G2", "B2", "D3"]]
  ]
}

How to Handle the "Timing" Variable in V1

Since your core objective is mastering timing, a raw list of sequential letters isn't quite enough—the data payload needs a way to express duration or grid placement. In a 4/4 song, a note could be a whole note (4 beats) or a quarter note (1 beat).

Two straightforward ways to model this in your V1 arrays depending on how you write your parser:

Approach A: The Quantized Grid (Step-Sequencer Style)

Every index in the array represents a fixed unit of time (e.g., one eighth note or one sixteenth note).

  • If a note is held, it can either repeat or use a hold character (_).
  • If nothing is played, it's a "Rest".
# Each element = One quarter-note beat
right_hand = [["C4"], ["Rest"], [["E4", "G4"]], ["C5"]]

Design Benefit: This maps beautifully to hardware/microcontroller clock cycles. Reading the array is just stepping through an iterator at a set tempo interval.

Approach B: Explicit Note-Duration Tuples

Instead of flat strings, every entry is an object or tuple declaring the pitch and how long it lasts.

right_hand = [
    {"pitches": ["C4"], "duration": "quarter"},
    {"pitches": ["E4", "G4"], "duration": "half"},
    {"pitches": ["Rest"], "duration": "quarter"}
]

Design Benefit: Closer to raw MIDI data structures. It keeps the arrays incredibly short because you don't need padding for empty space or held notes.

Decoupling pitch from time to get a baseline 100% accurate extraction is exactly how you validate the data pipeline. If the raw data isn't perfectly clean, any downstream layout engine you build will just be rendering perfectly formatted mistakes.

To achieve this, translating the image into an intermediate plain-text markup language like LilyPond or ABC notation is the standard industry approach. These languages are mature, deterministic, human-readable, and designed precisely to represent musical scores in code.

Using one of these as your intermediate representation handles the heavy lifting of structural formatting, allowing you to focus your code on parsing a clean string into your hand-specific arrays.

The Translation Architecture

[ Sheet Music Image ] 
          │
          ▼  (Vision Model / OMR API)
[ ABC Notation / LilyPond Text ]  <-- The Markdown Validation Checkpoint
          │
          ▼  (Your Custom Parser Script)
[ Hand-Separated Letter/Octave Arrays ]

Choosing the Intermediate Markdown

Option A: ABC Notation (Recommended for V1)

ABC notation is incredibly lightweight and reads like a raw string of characters. It handles pitches using case sensitivity and punctuation marks for octaves.

  • Pitches: C is Middle C ($C_4$). Lowercase c is an octave higher ($C_5$). A comma C, drops it an octave ($C_3$), and an apostrophe c' raises it ($c_6$).
  • Chords: Notes played simultaneously are simply wrapped in brackets [CEG].

Here is how a simple bar of piano music looks in ABC notation with separate tracks for the Left Hand (LH) and Right Hand (RH):

%%staves {RH LH}
V:RH clef=treble
[CEG] [DFA] [EGB] |
V:LH clef=bass
C,, G,, C, |

Option B: LilyPond (Better for Complicated Syntax)

LilyPond is essentially the $\LaTeX$ of music. It is highly structured but more verbose. It uses explicit octave markers (commas for low, apostrophes for high) and specifies absolute pitches.

\new PianoStaff <<
  \new Staff { \clef "treble" <c' e' g'> <d' f' a'> <e' g' b'> }
  \new Staff { \clef "bass" c, g, c }
>>

Why This Solves Your "Correctness" Problem

By forcing the software pipeline to output ABC notation or LilyPond first, you create a perfect debugging checkpoint.

  1. Human Verification: Since you already know how to identify chords by writing the letters down, you can instantly skim the text output to see if the vision model misread a note. [CEG] is explicitly a C Major chord—no staff lines blurring together.
  2. Deterministic Parsing: Writing a Python script to parse an ABC notation string like [CEG] into an array element ["C4", "E4", "G4"] is trivial regex and string manipulation. There is zero visual ambiguity left for your code to guess at.

Step 1 Code Implementation (The Parser)

If you feed your sheet music image to a multimodal vision model or an OMR tool and instruct it to "Convert this image strictly into ABC notation syntax," you will get back a clean text block.

From there, you can run a Python script to filter out the voices and map them into your raw sequential arrays. Here is a baseline pattern for how that string parsing looks:

import re

# Simulated output from your Image -> ABC text pipeline
abc_output = """
V:RH clef=treble
[CEG] c g [DFA]
V:LH clef=bass
C, G, C [F,A,C]
"""

def parse_abc_to_v1_arrays(abc_text):
    rh_notes = []
    lh_notes = []
    current_voice = None
    
    # Simple regex to catch chords like [CEG] or individual notes/tokens
    token_pattern = re.compile(r'\[[A-Ga-g,\']+\]|[A-Ga-g,\']+|Rest')

    for line in abc_text.strip().split('\n'):
        if line.startswith('V:RH'):
            current_voice = 'RH'
            continue
        elif line.startswith('V:LH'):
            current_voice = 'LH'
            continue
            
        if current_voice:
            # Find all notes or chord blocks in the line
            tokens = token_pattern.findall(line)
            for token in tokens:
                # Clean up brackets for chords
                cleaned = token.replace('[', '').replace(']', '')
                # If it's a chord, split into a list of notes, else keep as single element list
                note_element = list(cleaned) if len(cleaned) > 1 else [cleaned]
                
                if current_voice == 'RH':
                    rh_notes.append(note_element)
                else:
                    lh_notes.append(note_element)
                    
    return {"right_hand": rh_notes, "left_hand": lh_notes}

data_payload = parse_abc_to_v1_arrays(abc_output)
print(data_payload)
# Output: {'right_hand': [['C', 'E', 'G'], ['c'], ['g'], ['D', 'F', 'A']], 'left_hand': [['C', ','], ['G', ','], ['C'], ['F', ',', 'A', ',', 'C']]}

(Note: You can easily add a helper dictionary to this script to translate ABC's case-sensitive octaves like c or C, into your explicit scientific octave numbers like C5 or C3 during the cleanup phase).
